title: Containers and Images
objectives: Explain what a container isolates and what it shares with the host
Read an image as layers addressed by digest
Build small, reproducible, non-root images

cards.title: A process with a fenced-off view
cards.body: A container is an ordinary process that the kernel gives its own view of the filesystem, process list and network (namespaces) and a resource budget (control groups). It shares the host’s kernel, which is why containers usually start in well under a second and why a kernel bug can affect all of them.

cards.title: Images are stacked layers
cards.body: An image is a list of filesystem layers plus configuration (command, environment, user). Each build step that changes files adds a layer. Layers are identified by the hash of their content, so identical layers are stored and downloaded once and shared between images.

cards.title: Worked example: a multi-stage build
cards.body: A service needs a compiler to build but only the binary to run.
steps: Stage 1 starts from a full build image, copies the dependency manifest and installs dependencies (cached while the manifest is unchanged)
It then copies the source and compiles the binary
Stage 2 starts from a minimal runtime image
It copies only the binary from stage 1 and sets a non-root user
The final image drops the compiler and source, often shrinking from about 1 GB to tens of MB (illustrative)

cards.title: Misconception: a container is a lightweight virtual machine
cards.body: A virtual machine runs its own kernel on virtual hardware; a container runs on the host kernel. That makes containers lighter but gives a weaker isolation boundary, so multi-tenant platforms often add a VM or sandbox layer around untrusted containers.

cards.title: Trap: deploying by mutable tag
cards.body: Tags such as latest or v2 can be moved to point at a different image. Two nodes pulling “v2” an hour apart may run different code. Deploy by digest (sha256:…) or treat tags as immutable in your registry.

questions.prompt: What do containers on one host share?

choices.label: One network address for each process
A single filesystem with no isolation
The host’s operating system kernel
One process id for all containers

questions.explanation: Containers share the host kernel, and namespaces only give each one its own view. Each container gets its own network namespace and address, its own filesystem view and its own process ids, so the other options describe the isolation containers do have.

questions.prompt: Why copy the dependency manifest and install before copying source code?

choices.label: So the source files are left out of the final image
So the dependency layer stays cached
So the dependencies are pinned to exact versions
So the build steps can run in parallel

questions.explanation: Layers are cached in order, and the first changed layer invalidates everything after it. Source changes often and the manifest rarely, so installing first keeps the slow dependency layer cached. Leaving source out of the image is what a multi-stage build does, pinning comes from the lock file, and layer order does not make steps parallel.

questions.prompt: Which reference picks one exact image for every pull?

choices.label: A sha256 digest
The repository name alone
The latest tag
A version tag such as v2

questions.explanation: A digest is a hash of the image content, so it always names the same bytes. Tags, including latest and version tags like v2, are movable pointers that can be re-pushed, and a bare repository name resolves to the latest tag.

questions.prompt: Why run the container process as a non-root user?

choices.label: It gives the container its own kernel instead of the host one
It lets the image be pulled without registry credentials
It stops the container using more memory than its limit
An escape then gains fewer privileges

questions.explanation: If an attacker escapes a non-root process, they land with an unprivileged user rather than one that may map to root on the host. The kernel is shared whatever the user, pulls depend on registry auth, and memory limits come from control groups, not the user id.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a cache-friendly multi-stage build.

items.label: Copy only the built artefact and set a non-root user
Start a minimal runtime stage
Copy the dependency manifest and install dependencies
Copy the source and compile

questions.explanation: Stable layers first, then build, then a slim runtime.

questions.prompt: A platform runs code uploaded by many different customers on shared hosts.

approaches.label: Run each customer’s code as a process on the host
Plain containers sharing the host kernel
Containers inside lightweight VMs or a sandboxed runtime

rationaleOptions.label: Namespaces alone isolate untrusted code well
Processes on the host are as isolated as containers
Lightweight VMs still start quickly
A kernel exploit in one tenant does not reach the host directly

rationaleConflicts.r3: All containers share one kernel, so a kernel bug crosses tenants.
rationaleConflicts.r4: They see the host’s filesystem and processes.

questions.explanation: Containers package software; add a VM or sandbox boundary for untrusted tenants.

flashcards.back: A process with its own namespaces and cgroup limits, sharing the host kernel.
Content-addressed layers plus configuration.
Tags can move; a digest names exact content.

mechanism.title: What happens when a container starts
steps: The runtime pulls the image manifest by tag or digest, then downloads any layers it does not already have. Each layer is verified against its content hash, so a corrupted or tampered layer is rejected.

Layers are stacked with a union filesystem: lower layers are read-only and shared by every container from that image; each container gets a thin writable layer on top. Files changed at run time are lost when the container is removed unless written to a volume.
The runtime creates namespaces (mount, process id, network, user, hostname, IPC) so the process sees its own filesystem root, its own process tree starting at PID 1 and its own network interfaces.
Control groups cap and account for CPU, memory and I/O. A memory limit is enforced by the kernel: exceeding it gets the process killed, which surfaces as exit code 137.

Security settings narrow what the process may do: dropping Linux capabilities, a seccomp filter on system calls, a read-only root filesystem and a non-root user. Each limits the damage of a compromised application.

Because the image fixes the filesystem and the configuration, the same digest behaves the same on a laptop, in CI and in production, which is the main operational benefit: environment drift moves into a versioned artefact.

Registries store images by repository and digest. Signing images and verifying signatures at deploy time, together with scanning layers for known vulnerabilities, ties what runs in production back to a trusted build.

useWhen: Use containers to ship one reproducible artefact through every environment.
Use multi-stage builds and minimal base images for production.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on container isolation alone for untrusted code.
Avoid storing state in the container’s writable layer.
Avoid baking secrets or environment-specific configuration into images; inject them at run time.

rows: No shell; debug with separate tools
Needs tooling to map to versions

numbers.title: What a smaller image saves at scale
assumptions: Image shrinks from 900 MB to 60 MB with a multi-stage build (illustrative)
A scale-out event starts 200 new nodes, each pulling the image over 1 Gbit/s
steps: At 1 Gbit/s (about 125 MB/s), 900 MB takes about 7.2 s and 60 MB about 0.5 s per node.
Across 200 nodes the registry serves 180 GB versus 12 GB.
Fewer packages also means fewer vulnerability alerts to triage.
Faster pulls shorten how long new capacity takes to arrive during a spike.
numbers.result: Image size shows up as startup time, registry load and patching work.

india.title: The OCI image format
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Open Container Initiative maintains open specifications for container images, runtimes and distribution, so images built by one tool run on another runtime. An OCI image consists of a manifest, a configuration and a set of filesystem layers, each referenced by a cryptographic digest of its content. Docker’s documentation recommends multi-stage builds, minimal base images and pinning base images by digest for reproducible builds.

pitfalls.trap: “Containers are as isolated as VMs.”
pitfalls.say: “They share the host kernel; for untrusted code I’d add a VM or sandbox boundary.”

pitfalls.trap: “We deploy latest so we always get the newest build.”
pitfalls.say: “Latest can differ between nodes; I’d deploy an immutable digest.”

takeaways: A container is a fenced process sharing the host kernel.
Images are content-addressed layers; order them stable to volatile.
Deploy by digest; run as non-root.
Multi-stage builds ship only what runs.

interactive.title: What happens to the secret?
interactive.prompt: A build copies an .env file containing an API key in step 3, uses it, and deletes it in step 5. The image is pushed to a registry that several teams can pull from.

choices.label: Anyone who can pull the image can extract the key from step 3’s layer
choices.feedback: Right: deleting a file adds a layer that hides it but does not remove it.

choices.label: The key is gone because step 5 deleted it
choices.feedback: Earlier layers stay in the image unchanged.

choices.label: Registries strip secrets automatically on push
choices.feedback: Registries store layers as they are.

interactive.reveal: Use build-time secret mounts that never enter a layer, and rotate the exposed key.

Processes, which containers are built from

title: Running Containers on an Orchestrator
objectives: Describe how an orchestrator reconciles desired state
Use liveness, readiness and startup probes correctly
Set resource requests and limits and read their effects

cards.title: Declare what you want, not how
cards.body: You tell an orchestrator such as Kubernetes the desired state, for example “3 replicas of image X with 512 MiB each”. Controllers keep comparing actual with desired state and act on any difference: start a replacement for a crashed container, reschedule from a failed node.

cards.title: Three different probes
cards.body: A readiness probe decides whether a container receives traffic; failing it removes the pod from load balancing without restarting it. A liveness probe decides whether to restart a stuck container. A startup probe holds the other probes off until a slow-starting app has finished initialising.

cards.title: Worked example: probes for a service that warms a cache
cards.body: The service takes 40 s to load a cache at start and depends on a database.
steps: Startup probe: check /healthz every 5 s, allow up to 12 failures (60 s) before giving up
Readiness probe: return ready only once the cache is loaded and the process can serve requests
Liveness probe: check only that the process is responsive, not the database
If the database is down, readiness may fail, but liveness keeps passing so pods are not restarted in a loop
Pods rejoin traffic as soon as readiness passes again

cards.title: Misconception: liveness should check dependencies
cards.body: If liveness fails when the database is slow, every pod restarts at once, adding cold starts to a database incident. Restarting the app cannot fix a dependency. Keep liveness about the process itself.

cards.title: Trap: no requests, or limits far below real use
cards.body: Without CPU and memory requests the scheduler packs pods blindly and nodes run out under load. A memory limit below real peak usage gets the container killed (OOMKilled); a low CPU limit throttles it, adding latency without any error.

questions.prompt: A pod is alive but temporarily cannot serve. Which probe should fail?

choices.label: Liveness and readiness together
Startup
Readiness
Liveness

questions.explanation: Readiness failing removes the pod from service endpoints without restarting it, which is right for a temporary inability to serve. Liveness failing restarts the container, which is wrong for a pod that will recover on its own, so failing both adds a needless restart. Startup probes only gate the first start.

questions.prompt: Liveness checks the database. The database slows for 2 minutes. What happens?

choices.label: Pods are marked unready and keep running
Pods restart, adding load during the incident
Traffic shifts to another region
Pods keep serving from cache until the database recovers

questions.explanation: A liveness probe that checks a dependency fails for every pod at once, so the kubelet restarts them all while the database is slow, adding cold starts and reconnect load. Unready-but-running is what a readiness probe would cause. Kubernetes does not fail over regions, and the probe failure stops cached serving by restarting the process.

questions.prompt: A container exceeds its memory limit. What does the kernel do?

choices.label: Slows it down until usage drops
Writes the excess to swap quietly
Moves it to a larger node
Kills it; the pod reports OOMKilled

questions.explanation: Memory cannot be taken back from a process, so exceeding the limit gets the container OOM-killed and restarted. Slowing down is what happens at a CPU limit (throttling), swap is normally off for Kubernetes nodes, and the scheduler never moves a running pod to another node.

questions.prompt: A node fails with 3 replicas of your service on it. What does the controller do?

choices.label: Restarts the failed node’s kernel
Waits for an operator to approve new replicas
Reduces the desired replica count
Starts replacements on healthy nodes

questions.explanation: The controller compares desired with actual replicas and creates new pods, which the scheduler places on healthy nodes. It cannot touch the failed node’s kernel, needs no approval, and never lowers the desired count; only a person or an autoscaler changes that.

questions.prompt: Order what happens as a new pod comes up.

items.label: Readiness probe passes
Pod is added to service endpoints and receives traffic
Container starts
Startup probe passes

questions.explanation: Start, initialise, become ready, receive traffic.

questions.prompt: A latency-sensitive API has occasional CPU bursts during traffic spikes.

approaches.label: No requests or limits at all
Tight CPU limit equal to the request
Set accurate CPU and memory requests, a memory limit, and a generous or no CPU limit

rationaleOptions.label: Leaving resources unspecified lets the scheduler optimise
Scheduling reserves the CPU it needs
A tight CPU limit protects latency
Bursts use spare CPU instead of being throttled

rationaleConflicts.r3: Throttling during bursts is what raises p99.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Without requests it cannot place pods sensibly.

questions.explanation: Requests drive scheduling; memory limits prevent runaway use; tight CPU limits throttle bursts.

flashcards.back: Readiness gates traffic; liveness triggers restarts.
Delays other probes until a slow app has started.
Memory: killed. CPU: throttled.

sources.title: Kubernetes: Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes
Kubernetes: Resource Management for Pods and Containers

mechanism.title: The control loop behind an orchestrator
steps: You submit objects (Deployments, Services) to an API server, which stores them. Nothing happens directly; controllers watch those objects and work to make reality match.

The Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet, which creates pods. The scheduler assigns each pod to a node with enough unreserved CPU and memory, based on the pod’s requests, and on the node an agent (the kubelet) starts the containers.

The kubelet runs probes. A failing readiness probe removes the pod’s address from the Service’s endpoints; a failing liveness probe restarts the container; a startup probe disables the other two until it succeeds.

Requests are what the scheduler reserves; limits are what the kernel enforces. Over a memory limit the container is killed and restarted; over a CPU limit it is throttled within each scheduling period. A pod is in the Guaranteed quality-of-service class only when every container sets requests equal to limits for both CPU and memory. Under node memory pressure the kubelet first evicts pods using more memory than they requested, so BestEffort and over-request Burstable pods go before Guaranteed ones.

Rolling updates create new pods and remove old ones as new pods become ready, governed by maxSurge and maxUnavailable. Readiness is what makes a rolling update safe; a pod that reports ready too early receives traffic it cannot serve.

When a pod is deleted, it is removed from endpoints and sent SIGTERM at about the same time, then SIGKILL after the grace period, 30 seconds by default. Applications should keep serving briefly and shut down cleanly within that window.
Pod disruption budgets limit how many replicas voluntary actions such as node upgrades may take down at once, so maintenance cannot remove all healthy copies of a service at the same time.

useWhen: Use readiness probes on every service that receives traffic.
Use startup probes for slow initialisation instead of long liveness delays.
Use pod disruption budgets for services that must keep a minimum number of replicas during node maintenance.
avoidWhen: Avoid liveness probes that test dependencies.
Avoid running production pods without resource requests.

rows: One leak can starve the node

numbers.title: How many pods fit on a node
assumptions: Node: 8 CPU and 32 GiB allocatable (illustrative)
Pod requests 500m CPU and 1.5 GiB memory
steps: By CPU: 8 ÷ 0.5 = 16 pods.
By memory: 32 ÷ 1.5 ≈ 21 pods.
CPU is the binding constraint: 16 pods per node.
For 100 pods you need at least 7 nodes, before headroom for failures and rolling updates.
numbers.result: Requests decide packing; the scarcer resource sets how many pods fit.

india.title: What the Kubernetes documentation says about probes
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Kubernetes documentation on probes describes the three types: liveness probes decide when to restart a container, readiness probes decide when a container is ready to start accepting traffic, and startup probes disable liveness and readiness checks until the application has started. It cautions that liveness probes must be configured carefully, because incorrect ones can cause cascading failures and restart containers under high load.

pitfalls.trap: “Our liveness probe checks every dependency, to be safe.”
pitfalls.say: “That restarts healthy pods when a dependency blips; I’d check dependencies in readiness, if at all.”

pitfalls.trap: “We set CPU limits tight to protect latency.”
pitfalls.say: “Tight CPU limits throttle bursts; I’d set accurate requests and loosen the CPU limit.”

takeaways: Orchestrators reconcile desired state continuously.
Readiness gates traffic; liveness restarts; startup delays both.
Requests schedule; memory limits kill; CPU limits throttle.
Graceful shutdown must fit the termination grace period.

interactive.title: What happens during the database outage?
interactive.prompt: Each pod’s liveness probe calls the database with a 1 s timeout. The database becomes slow for 3 minutes.

choices.label: Pods fail liveness and restart repeatedly, adding cold-start load
choices.feedback: Right: liveness tied to a dependency turns its slowdown into a restart storm.

choices.label: Pods stop receiving traffic but stay running
choices.feedback: That would happen with readiness, not liveness.

choices.label: Nothing: probes ignore dependency timeouts
choices.feedback: The probe calls the database, so its timeouts fail the probe.

interactive.reveal: Move dependency checks out of liveness; keep liveness about the process.

title: CI/CD Pipelines
objectives: Explain continuous integration, delivery and deployment
Design a pipeline that builds once and promotes the same artefact
Use DORA’s software delivery metrics to judge delivery performance

cards.title: Integrate small changes often
cards.body: Continuous integration means everyone merges small changes into the main branch frequently, at least daily, and each merge triggers an automated build and test. Problems surface within minutes of the change that caused them, while the author still remembers it.

cards.title: Delivery versus deployment
cards.body: Continuous delivery keeps main always releasable: every passing build produces an artefact that could go to production with one approval. Continuous deployment removes that approval: passing builds go out automatically, guarded by tests, canaries and fast rollback.

cards.title: Worked example: a build-once pipeline
cards.body: A service moves from merge to production.
steps: On merge, CI builds one container image and tags it with the commit hash
Unit and integration tests run against that image
The same image digest deploys to staging; smoke tests run
After approval or automatic checks, the same digest deploys to production gradually
Rollback redeploys the previous digest; nothing is rebuilt

cards.title: Misconception: more manual approval makes releases safer
cards.body: Long approval chains batch many changes into big, rare releases, and big releases are harder to test, review and roll back. Small, frequent, automated releases tend to fail less and recover faster, as DORA’s research has repeatedly found.

cards.title: Trap: rebuilding for each environment
cards.body: If staging and production each build from source, they can pick up different dependency versions or build flags, so what you tested is not what you ship. Build once and promote the artefact; inject environment differences as configuration.

questions.prompt: What separates continuous deployment from continuous delivery?

choices.label: Every change must pass automated tests before merge
Artefacts are built once and promoted between environments
Staging is a copy of production configuration
No manual approval before production

questions.explanation: Both practices keep main releasable with automated tests and promoted artefacts; continuous deployment also removes the manual approval and releases every passing change. Tests before merge, build-once promotion and production-like staging belong to both, so they do not tell them apart.

questions.prompt: Why promote one artefact through all environments?

choices.label: Staging tests can then run in parallel with the production deploy
Production runs exactly what was tested
Each environment no longer needs its own configuration
Each environment can build from its own branch

questions.explanation: Promoting one artefact means production runs the exact bytes that passed the tests; rebuilding can pull different dependencies. Configuration still differs per environment and is injected at deploy time. Running staging tests in parallel with production defeats the gate, and per-environment branches are the drift this practice prevents.

questions.prompt: A team merges feature branches once a month. What problem is most likely?

choices.label: Too many small builds to review
Large, painful merges and late test failures
Too little disk space on the build servers for branches
Faster feedback than they can use

questions.explanation: Long-lived branches drift apart, so integration problems surface late as big merges and test failures. Monthly merges mean fewer builds and slower feedback, not more, and branches use little build-server disk.

questions.prompt: Which is one of DORA’s software delivery metrics?

choices.label: Test coverage of the main branch
Mean time between failures
Change failure rate
Story points completed per sprint

questions.explanation: Change fail rate is one of DORA’s software delivery metrics, with deployment frequency, change lead time, failed deployment recovery time and deployment rework rate. Coverage is a code metric, mean time between failures is a hardware-style reliability measure that DORA does not use, and story points measure planning, not delivery.

questions.prompt: Order a build-once pipeline.

items.label: Deploy the same digest to staging
Build the image once from the merged commit
Run tests against that image
Promote the same digest to production

questions.explanation: Build, test, stage, promote, without rebuilding.

questions.prompt: A 40-person team ships monthly releases that often break and take days to fix.

approaches.label: Release quarterly to allow more testing
Trunk-based development with automated tests and small daily deploys
Add a second manual QA phase

rationaleOptions.label: Problems are found while the change is fresh
Smaller changes are easier to test and roll back
More gates catch more bugs
Releasing less often reduces failures

rationaleConflicts.r3: They also batch more changes, making each release riskier.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Bigger batches fail in harder-to-diagnose ways.

questions.explanation: Reduce batch size and automate checks; speed and stability improve together.

flashcards.back: Merge small changes to main often; each merge is built and tested.
One artefact promoted through every environment.
Deployment frequency, change lead time, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate and deployment rework rate.

sources.title: Google Cloud: DORA’s software delivery metrics

mechanism.title: Anatomy of a delivery pipeline
steps: Trigger: each push or merge starts a pipeline defined as code in the repository, so its changes are reviewed like any other code.
Build: compile and package into one immutable artefact, recorded by digest. Fast feedback matters most here: aim for a commit-to-result time of minutes, splitting slow suites into later stages.

Test: unit tests first, then integration and contract tests against the built artefact, then security scans of dependencies and the image. Flaky tests must be fixed or quarantined quickly, or people learn to ignore failures.

Release: deploy the artefact to staging, run smoke tests, then to production with a progressive strategy (canary or rolling) and automatic rollback on bad health signals. Feature flags let code ship dark and be enabled separately from deploys.

Security of the pipeline: the pipeline holds deploy credentials, so restrict who can change it, avoid giving third-party build steps secrets, and record provenance so production can verify an artefact came from it.

Measure: DORA’s software delivery metrics, deployment frequency, change lead time, change fail rate, failed deployment recovery time and deployment rework rate, show whether changes to the pipeline actually improve delivery rather than just adding steps.

Rollback must be a routine, tested path: redeploying the previous artefact digest should take minutes and need no rebuild. Teams that practise it recover faster, which shows up directly in the time-to-restore metric.

useWhen: Use build-once, promote-everywhere pipelines.
Use trunk-based development with short-lived branches.
Use feature flags to separate deploying code from releasing a feature to users.
avoidWhen: Avoid manual steps that must be repeated per release.
Avoid pipelines that take hours before the first failure shows.
Avoid giving third-party build steps access to deploy credentials or production secrets.

numbers.title: Batch size and the cost of a bad release
assumptions: 30 changes per month; each has a 3% chance of causing an incident (illustrative)
Monthly release versus daily releases of about 1–2 changes
steps: Monthly: a release carries 30 changes; chance at least one is bad ≈ 1 − 0.97^30 ≈ 60%.
Finding the culprit means searching 30 changes.
Daily: each release carries 1–2 changes, so about 3–6% fail, and the culprit is obvious.
The total number of bad changes is the same; small batches make each one cheaper to find and undo.
numbers.result: Small batches do not remove defects; they make each one quick to locate and roll back.

india.title: DORA’s software delivery metrics
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Google Cloud’s DORA research programme has surveyed thousands of technology professionals over many years. For years it measured delivery with four keys: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service. It now uses five metrics in two groups, throughput (change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time) and instability (change fail rate, deployment rework rate), where rework rate counts unplanned deployments made to fix problems in production. Its reports consistently find that the highest performers do well on both speed and stability, rather than trading one for the other, and link this to practices such as continuous integration, trunk-based development and deployment automation.

pitfalls.trap: “We test thoroughly, so we release quarterly.”
pitfalls.say: “Large batches make releases riskier; I’d release smaller changes more often with automated checks.”

pitfalls.trap: “Staging passed, so production is identical.”
pitfalls.say: “Only if we promoted the same artefact; rebuilding per environment can change what ships.”

takeaways: Integrate small changes daily; build and test every merge.
Build once, promote the same digest.
Automate deploys with progressive rollout and rollback.
Track DORA’s delivery metrics for both speed and stability.

interactive.title: Why did production differ from staging?
interactive.prompt: Staging and production each run “build from main” in their own pipeline step, an hour apart. A dependency published a new minor version in between.

choices.label: Production picked up the new dependency version staging never tested
choices.feedback: Right: rebuilding per environment lets inputs drift.

choices.label: Staging and production hardware differ
choices.feedback: Possible in general, but this difference is in the build inputs.

choices.label: Nothing differs; builds from main are identical
choices.feedback: Only with a lockfile and a single build.

interactive.reveal: Build one artefact, pin dependencies, and promote that exact digest.

title: Progressive Delivery: Rolling, Blue-Green and Canary
objectives: Compare rolling, blue-green and canary releases
Size a canary so it detects a bad build quickly
Automate rollback from health signals

cards.title: Limit how many users meet a new version
cards.body: Progressive delivery exposes a change to a small share of traffic first, watches health signals, and widens exposure only if they stay good. The aim is that a bad build hurts a few users for a few minutes, not everyone at once.

cards.title: Three common strategies
cards.body: Rolling updates replace instances a few at a time. Blue-green runs a full second environment and switches all traffic at once, keeping the old one for instant rollback. Canary sends a small percentage of traffic to the new version and compares its error rate and latency with the old.

cards.title: Worked example: a canary plan
cards.body: A service handles 2,000 requests a minute.
steps: Stage 1: 5% of traffic for 15 minutes; compare error rate and p99 latency with the baseline
Stage 2: 25% for 15 minutes
Stage 3: 50%, then 100%
Any stage where errors exceed baseline by a set margin triggers automatic rollback
Database changes ship separately and stay compatible with both versions

cards.title: Misconception: a 1% canary is the safest choice
cards.body: A tiny canary limits exposure, but on a low-traffic service it sees so few requests that a bad build may produce too few errors to trip an alarm for a long time. Canary size must give enough traffic for a statistically clear signal in the time you allow.

cards.title: Trap: config and content pushed outside the pipeline
cards.body: Teams canary code but push configuration, feature flags or data files to every server at once. Many large outages came from exactly such global changes. Route them through the same staged rollout.

questions.prompt: Which strategy offers the fastest full rollback by switching traffic back?

choices.label: Recreate (stop all, start all)
Manual server-by-server patching
Blue-green
Rolling update

questions.explanation: Blue-green keeps the old environment running, so rollback is a traffic switch. A rolling update must roll every instance back, recreate has to restart the old version from scratch, and manual patching is slow in both directions.

questions.prompt: A canary at 1% on a low-traffic service shows no errors after 10 minutes. What is the risk?

choices.label: The baseline gets slower
The canary wastes capacity that the baseline needs
Users notice the version change
Too little traffic to reveal a bad build

questions.explanation: At 1% of a low-traffic service, ten minutes may see only a handful of requests, too few to show a bad error rate or latency. The baseline is not slowed and the canary takes little capacity; users noticing the change is not the risk the test is about.

questions.prompt: What must hold for a canary and the old version to run side by side?

choices.label: Both work with the same data schema
They run in the same availability zone
They each use their own separate database
The canary gets its own copy of the cache

questions.explanation: Both versions read and write the same data, so the schema must be compatible both ways during the rollout. They can run in any zones, separate databases or cache copies would split the data, and the code differs by definition.

questions.prompt: What should a canary compare against?

choices.label: Last month’s average error rate
The current version over the same period
The staging environment’s results from the same build
A fixed error budget for the year

questions.explanation: Comparing with the current version over the same minutes removes time-of-day and traffic-mix effects. Last month’s average and a yearly budget are not like-for-like, and staging results do not show production behaviour.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of an automated canary rollout.

items.label: Deploy the new version to a small share of traffic
Complete the rollout or roll back automatically
Compare its health signals with the baseline
Increase traffic in steps while signals stay healthy

questions.explanation: Expose, compare, widen, decide.

questions.prompt: A security agent update is pushed to millions of customer machines.

approaches.label: Let each customer test it themselves
Staged rings: internal, then a small customer share, then wider
Push to every machine at once for speed

rationaleOptions.label: Urgent updates still move fast through short stages
Customers will catch problems in their own tests
A crash appears in a small ring before reaching everyone
Urgent updates justify skipping stages

rationaleConflicts.r3: A fast global push turns one bad file into a global outage.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Most customers cannot test every update.

questions.explanation: Stage every change that can break machines, including content and config.

flashcards.back: Replace gradually; switch environments; route a small share first.
Enough traffic to detect a bad build within the time you allow.
Config, flags and content, not just code.

mechanism.title: Turning rollouts into experiments
steps: A canary is an experiment: the new version is the treatment, the old is the control, and both receive comparable traffic at the same time. Comparing at the same time removes the effect of traffic changes and time of day.

Choose metrics that reflect user harm: error rate, latency percentiles, saturation, and key business events such as successful checkouts. Crash loops and restarts are strong signals for agents and clients.

Detection time depends on traffic. The number of bad requests needed to trip an alert is roughly fixed, so a canary carrying 10 times more traffic trips it about 10 times faster, at the cost of exposing more users.

Rolling updates are progressive by instance count but often lack an explicit comparison; adding pauses and health gates between batches turns them into simple canaries. Blue-green trades double capacity during the switch for an instant rollback path.
Compatibility is a precondition: during a rollout both versions read and write the same data and talk to each other, so schema changes follow expand-then-contract and APIs stay backward compatible.

Everything that can break production deserves staging: binaries, configuration, feature-flag changes, security content and machine images. Global, instant pushes of any of them bypass the safety the pipeline provides.

useWhen: Use canaries with automatic analysis for high-traffic services.
Use blue-green when instant rollback matters and capacity allows.
avoidWhen: Avoid canaries too small to produce a signal in time.
Avoid pushing config or content globally while code goes through stages.

numbers.title: How canary size sets detection time
assumptions: Service: 2,000 requests a minute; a bad build fails 2% of its requests; the alarm fires after 20 failed requests (illustrative)
steps: At 1%: 20 requests a minute go to the canary, 0.4 fail a minute, so the alarm needs 50 minutes.
At 10%: 200 a minute, 4 fail a minute: 5 minutes.
At 50%: 1,000 a minute, 20 fail a minute: 1 minute, but half of users meet the bad build.
In every case about 20 users see an error before the alarm; size decides how long the experiment takes.
numbers.result: Pick the canary share that detects within your time budget; the failures before the alarm stay about the same.

india.title: A global content update
india.label: Publicly reported
india.body: Publicly reported by CrowdStrike and Microsoft in July 2024: a faulty configuration content update for CrowdStrike’s Falcon sensor was delivered to Windows hosts worldwide at once, crashing machines; Microsoft estimated about 8.5 million Windows devices were affected. CrowdStrike’s review said the content type had not gone through staged deployment and committed to staggered, ring-based rollouts with customer control over timing.

pitfalls.trap: “We did a canary, so the release was safe.”
pitfalls.say: “Only if the canary saw enough traffic to show a difference; I’d size it for the detection time we need.”

pitfalls.trap: “It’s just a config change, so we push it everywhere.”
pitfalls.say: “Config breaks production as easily as code; I’d stage it the same way.”

takeaways: Expose changes gradually and compare with the old version.
Canary size sets how quickly a bad build is detected.
Both versions must work with the same data during rollout.
Stage config and content as well as code.

interactive.title: Size the canary
interactive.prompt: A service gets 2,000 requests a minute. A bad build fails 2% of its requests, and the alarm fires after 20 failed requests (illustrative). Slide the share of traffic on the new version.
interactive.takeaway: Below about 5% this service needs over 10 minutes to detect a bad build; bigger canaries detect faster but expose more users per minute. About 20 users see errors before the alarm whatever the size.

seeAlso.why: Blue-green, canary and feature flags in system design
Schema changes compatible with both versions

title: Infrastructure as Code
objectives: Describe infrastructure declaratively and review it like code
Explain plan, apply, state and drift
Structure changes to limit blast radius

cards.title: Infrastructure in version control
cards.body: Infrastructure as code (IaC) describes networks, databases, permissions and services in files that are reviewed, versioned and applied by a tool. Environments become reproducible, changes have an author and a reason, and a lost region can be rebuilt from the repository.

cards.title: Plan, then apply
cards.body: Declarative tools compare the desired configuration with what exists (tracked in a state record) and produce a plan: create these, change those, destroy these. Reviewing the plan, not just the code diff, shows the real effect, including replacements that destroy data.

cards.title: Worked example: a safe change to a database
cards.body: An engineer changes a database setting in code.
steps: Open a pull request with the configuration change
CI runs the plan and posts it on the pull request
The plan shows “must be replaced” for the database: the change would destroy and recreate it
The team switches to a setting that can be updated in place, and enables deletion protection
After approval, CI applies the reviewed plan using a locked state file

cards.title: Misconception: the code is the truth
cards.body: Someone can change a resource by hand in the console, and the real infrastructure drifts from the code. The next apply may silently revert the fix or fail. Detect drift regularly and route every change through code.

cards.title: Trap: one huge state for everything
cards.body: Putting every environment and service in one configuration makes every plan slow and every apply risky: a typo can touch production networking while changing a test bucket. Split by environment and component so each apply has a small blast radius.

questions.prompt: What should a reviewer check before an IaC change is applied?

choices.label: The plan’s creates, updates and destroys
How clear the commit message is
Who wrote the change and how much experience they have
The size of the code diff in lines

questions.explanation: The plan shows what will really happen, including replacements and destroys that a small diff can hide. Commit message, author experience and diff size do not tell you whether a database will be replaced.

questions.prompt: A security group was edited by hand in the console. What is this called?

choices.label: Provisioning
Promotion
Rollback
Drift

questions.explanation: Drift is live infrastructure that no longer matches the declared configuration, often from console edits. Provisioning creates resources, promotion moves an artefact between environments, and rollback returns to a previous version.

questions.prompt: Why does the tool lock its state during apply?

choices.label: To make the apply reversible if it fails halfway
To stop the provider changing resources during the apply
To stop two applies changing it at once
To keep the plan from going stale after review

questions.explanation: The lock stops two applies writing state or changing the same resources at once. It does not make a failed apply reversible, cannot stop the cloud provider or anyone in the console from changing things, and a plan goes stale whenever the code or real resources change.

questions.prompt: Which change most limits the blast radius of an apply?

choices.label: Running plan and apply in a single CI step
One shared state covering all environments together
Pinning provider versions in every module
Separate states per environment and component

questions.explanation: Splitting state by environment and component means one apply can only touch that slice. One shared state puts everything in reach of every apply, merging plan and apply skips review, and pinning providers improves repeatability without limiting what an apply can change.

questions.prompt: Order a reviewed infrastructure change.

items.label: Reviewers approve the plan and code
Edit the configuration in a branch
CI applies the approved plan with a state lock
CI generates the plan

questions.explanation: Change, plan, review, apply.

questions.prompt: A company has hand-built production infrastructure and needs a second region for disaster recovery.

approaches.label: Write a document listing every setting
Click through the console again in the new region
Import existing resources into code, then create the second region from it

rationaleOptions.label: Future changes apply to both consistently
Both regions come from one reviewed definition
A settings document is as good as code
Console familiarity makes manual rebuilds reliable

rationaleConflicts.r3: Hundreds of settings make manual copies drift.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Documents go stale and are not applied automatically.

questions.explanation: Codify first; replication and recovery then become an apply.

flashcards.back: The tool’s list of changes needed to reach the declared state.
Real infrastructure differing from code because of out-of-band changes.
Prevents concurrent applies corrupting the state.

mechanism.title: How declarative infrastructure tools work
steps: You declare resources and their settings. The tool builds a dependency graph (a subnet before the server inside it) and keeps a state record mapping each declared resource to a real one by id.

Plan: the tool reads state, refreshes it from the provider’s APIs, and diffs against the configuration. Each resource gets an action: create, update in place, replace (destroy then create) or destroy.
Apply executes the plan in dependency order, in parallel where possible, and updates state. State must be stored remotely with locking, so two engineers or pipelines cannot apply at once.

Replacements are the dangerous action: some settings cannot change in place, so the tool destroys and recreates the resource. For data stores that means data loss unless protected by deletion protection or lifecycle rules that forbid destroy.

Drift happens through console edits, scripts and other tools. Scheduled plans that should show “no changes” detect it; the fix is to codify the change or revert it, then restrict console write access.
Modules package reusable patterns (a standard service, a network) with inputs, so teams compose infrastructure from reviewed building blocks instead of copying files.

Policy as code adds automated checks to plans before apply: no public storage buckets, encryption required on databases, approved instance types only. Violations fail the pipeline the same way a failing test does.

useWhen: Use IaC for anything you would need to rebuild after a disaster.
Use remote state with locking and CI-driven applies.
Use deletion protection and lifecycle rules on data stores managed by IaC.
avoidWhen: Avoid manual console changes in production.
Avoid one giant state covering every environment.
Avoid copying configuration between environments; use modules with per-environment inputs.

rows: Scripts must handle every existing state
Replacements if plans are not read

numbers.title: Rebuilding an environment
assumptions: Production has about 400 resources (illustrative)
Manual creation: about 5 minutes each; IaC apply: about 40 minutes total
steps: Manual: 400 × 5 = 2,000 minutes, about 33 hours of focused work.
With a few mistakes per hundred settings, several resources will differ from the original.
IaC: about 40 minutes of apply time, identical to the definition.
In a regional disaster, the difference is days versus an afternoon.
numbers.result: IaC turns a rebuild from days of manual work into one reviewed apply.

india.title: State and locking in Terraform
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: HashiCorp’s documentation explains that Terraform stores state about managed infrastructure to map real resources to configuration, track metadata and improve performance, and that teams should use remote state. If supported by the backend, Terraform locks state for all operations that could write it, preventing others from acquiring the lock and potentially corrupting state. The plan command shows the actions Terraform would take before anything changes.

pitfalls.trap: “The code was reviewed, so the apply is safe.”
pitfalls.say: “The code diff can hide a replacement; I’d review the plan, especially for data stores.”

pitfalls.trap: “It’s a quick fix, I’ll do it in the console.”
pitfalls.say: “That creates drift; I’d make the change in code so the next apply does not undo it.”

takeaways: Declare infrastructure in code and apply through CI.
Review plans, especially replacements.
Use remote, locked state split by blast radius.
Detect and remove drift regularly.

interactive.title: What does the next apply do?
interactive.prompt: An engineer opened a firewall port by hand in the console during an incident. The code still lists the old rules. A colleague applies an unrelated change from the same configuration.

choices.label: It closes the hand-opened port again
choices.feedback: Right: the tool reverts drift to match the code.

choices.label: It leaves the port open because it is unrelated
choices.feedback: The plan includes every difference in that state.

choices.label: It fails until the console change is deleted
choices.feedback: It simply plans an update back to the declared rules.

interactive.reveal: Codify incident fixes promptly, and read plans for unexpected changes.

Rebuilding a region in disaster recovery

title: SLIs, SLOs and Error Budgets
objectives: Define service level indicators from the user’s point of view
Set an SLO and compute its error budget
Use burn-rate alerts and an error-budget policy

cards.title: Measure what users feel
cards.body: A service level indicator (SLI) is a ratio of good events to valid events, such as the share of requests answered successfully within 300 ms. It should reflect user experience, not internal signals like CPU usage.

cards.title: Objectives and budgets
cards.body: A service level objective (SLO) is a target for an SLI over a window, such as 99.9% over 30 days. The remaining 0.1% is the error budget: the amount of unreliability you accept. While budget remains, teams ship; when it is spent, they prioritise reliability.

cards.title: Worked example: a 99.9% availability SLO
cards.body: An API serves 10 million requests in 30 days.
steps: SLI: successful responses ÷ valid requests, measured at the load balancer
SLO: 99.9% over a rolling 30 days
Error budget: 0.1% × 10,000,000 = 10,000 failed requests
In time terms: 0.1% of 30 days = 43.2 minutes of full outage
An incident that fails 4,000 requests uses 40% of the month’s budget

cards.title: Misconception: aim for 100%
cards.body: Users cannot tell 99.99% from 100% when their own network fails more often, and each extra nine costs far more engineering and slows releases. Pick the lowest target that keeps users happy; anything above it is budget for change.

cards.title: Trap: alerting on every error
cards.body: Paging someone for each error spike creates noise and fatigue. Alert on burn rate instead: how fast the error budget is being consumed. A fast burn pages; a slow burn files a ticket.

questions.prompt: Which is the best SLI for a checkout API?

choices.label: Number of checkout servers running
Share of checkout requests that succeed within 1 s
Average CPU use across all of the checkout servers
Size of the checkout database

questions.explanation: An SLI should measure what users experience, here checkout requests that succeed fast enough. Server count, CPU and database size are internal signals that can look fine while checkouts fail.

questions.prompt: An SLO is 99.95% availability over 30 days. How many minutes of full outage does the error budget allow?
assumptions: 30-day window
Full outage counts as all requests failing
questions.explanation: Design implication: one bad deploy that takes 15 minutes to roll back uses most of the month’s budget, so fast rollback matters as much as fewer incidents.

questions.prompt: The error budget for this month is spent. What does a typical error-budget policy say?

choices.label: Keep shipping features as planned
Pause risky launches and fix reliability
Raise the SLO target to motivate the team next month
Lower the SLO so the budget is no longer spent

questions.explanation: A typical policy pauses risky launches and spends effort on reliability until the budget recovers. Shipping as planned ignores the budget, raising the SLO makes it harder still, and lowering the SLO to clear the budget breaks the agreement it exists to protect.

questions.prompt: What does a burn rate of 10 mean for a 30-day budget?

choices.label: 10% of it has been used
10 incidents have happened
It lasts 10 times longer
It would be used up in about 3 days

questions.explanation: Burn rate is how fast the budget is spent relative to the even rate that lasts the whole window, so 10 means 30 days ÷ 10 = 3 days. It is not a percentage used, a count of incidents, or a longer-lasting budget.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to set up an SLO.

items.label: Pick the user journey that matters
Set the SLO target and window
Alert on error-budget burn rate
Define the SLI as good events over valid events

questions.explanation: Journey, indicator, objective, alerting.

questions.prompt: An on-call team gets 40 pages a week, most for brief error spikes that resolve themselves.

approaches.label: Multi-window burn-rate alerts on the SLO
Lower the error threshold so more spikes page
Turn off paging and check dashboards daily

rationaleOptions.label: Pages fire for sustained, budget-threatening problems
Daily dashboard checks are enough
Brief self-resolving spikes stop waking people
More sensitive thresholds catch more outages

rationaleConflicts.r3: They add noise, and noisy pagers get ignored.
rationaleConflicts.r4: A fast outage can burn the budget within hours.

questions.explanation: Alert on what threatens the SLO, at a speed that matches the threat.

flashcards.back: Good events ÷ valid events, measured where users feel it.
About 43 minutes of full outage.
How many times faster than sustainable the budget is being spent.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Service Level Objectives
Google SRE Workbook: Alerting on SLOs
Google SRE Workbook: Error Budget Policy

mechanism.title: From indicators to decisions
steps: Choose a few critical user journeys (log in, search, check out) and define one or two SLIs each, typically availability and latency. Measure as close to the user as practical: load balancer logs or client telemetry rather than server internals.
Define each SLI as a ratio of good to valid events. Excluding invalid events (such as requests rejected for bad input) keeps the indicator about the service’s own behaviour.
Set the SLO from user expectations and historical performance. Use a rolling window (often 28 or 30 days) so a bad day stays visible for a while, but not forever.
The error budget is 1 − SLO. It turns reliability into a shared, measurable quantity: product and engineering agree in advance what happens when it runs low, which removes arguments during incidents.

Alert on burn rate. A burn rate of 1 spends exactly the budget over the window; the SRE Workbook suggests paging when, for example, 2% of a 30-day budget is spent in one hour (burn rate about 14.4), and filing tickets for slower burns, using a long and a short window together to avoid flapping.
Review SLOs periodically: if users complain while the SLO is met, the SLI measures the wrong thing; if the budget is never touched, the target may be too strict and slowing delivery for no benefit.

useWhen: Use SLOs to decide between feature work and reliability work.
Use burn-rate alerting for paging.
Use the same SLIs on dashboards, alerts and reviews.
avoidWhen: Avoid SLIs based on machine metrics such as CPU.
Avoid targets stricter than users need or your dependencies can support.

rows: Room for frequent change and manual fixes
Automated rollback, on-call response in minutes
Redundancy everywhere; humans too slow to react

numbers.title: Burn rate in practice
assumptions: SLO 99.9% over 30 days: budget 43.2 minutes of full outage
An incident fails 5% of requests
steps: Burn rate = error rate ÷ budget rate = 5% ÷ 0.1% = 50.
At burn rate 50, the 30-day budget lasts 30 days ÷ 50 = 0.6 days, about 14 hours.
In one hour it spends 1 ÷ 14.4 of the budget, about 7%, well above a 2%-per-hour paging threshold.
A 0.2% error rate is burn rate 2: a ticket, not a page.
numbers.result: Burn rate converts any error rate into “how soon is the budget gone”, which sets alert urgency.

india.title: Error budgets in Google’s SRE practice
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Google’s Site Reliability Engineering book describes the error budget as one minus the SLO, and explains that as long as the measured uptime is above the SLO, new releases can be pushed. Its workbook includes an example error budget policy: if a service has exceeded its error budget for the preceding four-week window, all changes and releases other than urgent fixes and security patches are halted until the service is back within its SLO.

pitfalls.trap: “We target 100% uptime.”
pitfalls.say: “That leaves no budget for change and isn’t measurable against real networks; I’d set an SLO users actually need.”

pitfalls.trap: “We alert whenever errors exceed 1%.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d alert on burn rate so short blips don’t page and sustained problems do.”

takeaways: SLIs measure user-visible good events over valid events.
Error budget = 1 − SLO; spend it on change.
Page on fast burn rates, ticket on slow ones.
Agree on an error-budget policy before incidents.

interactive.title: Should this page someone at 3 a.m.?
interactive.prompt: SLO: 99.9% over 30 days. For the last 10 minutes, 0.3% of requests have failed; the previous hour was normal.

choices.label: No: burn rate 3 is worth a ticket, not a page
choices.feedback: Right: at that rate the budget would last 10 days.

choices.label: Yes: any error rate above the SLO pages
choices.feedback: That pages on noise; urgency depends on burn rate.

choices.label: No: errors under 1% never matter
choices.feedback: They matter if sustained; that is what the ticket is for.

interactive.reveal: Page on fast burns such as 2% of the budget in an hour; ticket on slow ones.

seeAlso.why: Logging and metrics for services
Incidents are where the error budget is spent

title: Incident Response and Postmortems
objectives: Run an incident with clear roles
Prioritise mitigation over diagnosis
Write a blameless postmortem with useful actions

cards.title: Roles stop chaos
cards.body: In an incident, an incident commander coordinates and decides; an operations lead makes changes; a communications lead updates stakeholders; someone keeps a timeline. Separating these lets the people fixing the system focus while others handle questions.

cards.title: Mitigate first, diagnose later
cards.body: The first goal is to stop user harm: roll back the last deploy, fail over, shed load, disable a feature flag. Finding the root cause can wait until users are no longer affected; long investigations during an outage extend it.

cards.title: Worked example: the first 15 minutes
cards.body: Error rates jump on checkout shortly after a deploy.
steps: Page fires; the first responder declares an incident and becomes commander
Commander opens a channel, assigns an ops lead and a communications lead
Ops lead checks recent changes: a deploy 10 minutes ago
Commander decides to roll back now rather than debug the new version
Errors recover; the team keeps monitoring, updates the status page, then starts the timeline for the postmortem

cards.title: Misconception: postmortems find who made the mistake
cards.body: Blaming people makes others hide information, which hides the real weaknesses. Blameless postmortems assume people acted reasonably with what they knew, and ask which tools, checks and designs allowed a normal mistake to become an outage.

cards.title: Trap: action items nobody owns
cards.body: Postmortems often end with vague actions such as “be more careful” or “improve monitoring” with no owner or date. Good actions are specific, owned, tracked and prioritised, for example “add input validation to the capacity tool so it refuses to remove more than 5% of servers”.

questions.prompt: Errors spike 5 minutes after a deploy. What is usually the first move?

choices.label: Write a postmortem draft
Add more logging and redeploy
Read the diff line by line
Roll back the deploy

questions.explanation: When errors follow a deploy, rolling back is usually the fastest way to stop the harm; diagnosis can follow. Reading the diff or adding logging extends the outage, and the postmortem comes after recovery.

questions.prompt: What does the incident commander mainly do?

choices.label: Answers each customer email about the outage
Types every fix into production
Writes the code for the fix
Coordinates people and makes decisions

questions.explanation: The commander coordinates the response, assigns roles and makes decisions. Fixes are done by the operations lead and others, and customer updates go through the communications lead.

questions.prompt: Which postmortem action is most useful?

choices.label: Make the tool refuse large server removals
Record that the operator made an error
Remind all engineers to be more careful
Retrain the operator on the tool before they use it again

questions.explanation: A guard in the tool prevents the same mistake by anyone. Recording an operator error, reminding people to be careful and retraining one person rely on humans never slipping, so the same failure can recur.

questions.prompt: Why are postmortems blameless?

choices.label: So the postmortem can be finished within a day
So the incident does not count against the error budget
So no one has to own the action items afterwards
So people share what really happened

questions.explanation: When people are not punished they share what they saw and did, which exposes the system causes. Blamelessness does not make a review faster, does not change the error budget, and action items still need named owners.

questions.prompt: Order the incident lifecycle.

items.label: Resolve and verify recovery
Detect and declare the incident
Mitigate user impact
Assign roles and communicate
Write and review the postmortem

questions.explanation: Declare, organise, mitigate, resolve, learn.

questions.prompt: A database is overloaded and the cause is unclear. Customers cannot log in.

approaches.label: Restart the database primary immediately
Shed non-critical load (disable heavy features) while investigating
Keep everything on until the root cause is found

rationaleOptions.label: Changing anything before diagnosis is risky
Restores logins quickly by reducing pressure
Buys time to investigate safely
A restart fixes overload

rationaleConflicts.r3: Users are already affected; reversible mitigation is low risk.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Restarts can lose caches and make the overload worse.

questions.explanation: Prefer reversible mitigations that reduce harm now.

flashcards.back: Coordinates the response and decides; does not do hands-on fixes.
Mitigate user impact before root-causing.
Focus on systemic causes and owned actions, not on people.

mechanism.title: Structure that holds up under pressure
steps: Declare early. Declaring an incident is cheap and can be downgraded; waiting until certain wastes the first minutes, which are often the most valuable.

Set up roles and one communication channel. The commander keeps a running summary: what we know, what we are trying, the next update time. Status updates to customers go out on a regular cadence even when there is no news.

Mitigation options are prepared in advance: rollback, feature flags, failover, traffic shifting, load shedding, scaling out. Runbooks list them per service so responders choose rather than invent under stress.
Keep a timeline as you go: detection time, key observations, decisions and changes with timestamps. It is the backbone of the postmortem and avoids reconstructing events from memory.

After recovery, write a postmortem: impact, timeline, contributing factors, what went well, where we got lucky, and action items with owners and priorities. Review it widely; share lessons across teams.
Track metrics over time: time to detect, time to mitigate, and repeat incidents. Repeats mean action items are not being completed or not addressing the real weakness.

Paging and escalation policies decide who is woken and when: a primary on-call, a secondary if the primary does not acknowledge within minutes, and clear rules for pulling in other teams. Handovers at shift changes include the current summary, so context is not lost.

useWhen: Use clear roles for any incident with user impact.
Use reversible mitigations before deep diagnosis.
Use a status page and a fixed update cadence for incidents customers can see.
avoidWhen: Avoid one person both fixing and coordinating.
Avoid postmortems that name individuals as the cause.
Avoid closing action items without checking they removed the weakness they targeted.

numbers.title: Where incident minutes go
assumptions: Example incident: 8 minutes to detect, 25 to decide on rollback, 5 to roll back (illustrative)
Fixed costs: detection and rollback mechanics
steps: User impact lasts 8 + 25 + 5 = 38 minutes.
Most of it, 25 minutes, is deliberation before mitigating.
A rule “roll back first if a deploy happened in the last hour” cuts that to about 2 minutes: impact ≈ 15 minutes.
Faster detection helps, but decision rules often save more.
numbers.result: Decide on mitigations by rule, not by debate, to cut user impact.

india.title: One command, many servers
india.label: Publicly reported
india.body: Publicly reported by Amazon Web Services in its summary of the 28 February 2017 Amazon S3 disruption in the US-EAST-1 region: while debugging a billing system, an authorised team member ran a command intended to remove a small number of servers, but one input was entered incorrectly and a larger set was removed, including servers supporting critical subsystems. Restarting them took hours. AWS changed the tool to remove capacity more slowly and to block removals that would take a subsystem below its minimum capacity.

pitfalls.trap: “Let’s find the root cause before touching anything.”
pitfalls.say: “Users are affected now; I’d roll back or shed load first, then investigate.”

pitfalls.trap: “The engineer made a typo; that’s the root cause.”
pitfalls.say: “A typo was the trigger; the root cause is a tool that allowed it to remove that much capacity.”

takeaways: Declare early, assign roles, communicate on a cadence.
Mitigate user impact before diagnosing.
Keep a timeline during the incident.
Blameless postmortems with specific, owned actions.

interactive.title: What should the commander do?
interactive.prompt: Ten minutes into an outage, two engineers are debating which of three recent changes caused it. One of the changes is a deploy that can be rolled back in 2 minutes.

choices.label: Roll back the deploy now, then continue investigating
choices.feedback: Right: a cheap, reversible mitigation beats more debate.

choices.label: Let the debate continue until there is agreement
choices.feedback: Users stay affected while it continues.

choices.label: Roll back all three changes and a week of others
choices.feedback: Broad rollbacks add risk; start with the cheapest likely fix.

interactive.reveal: Prefer the quickest reversible mitigation, then confirm its effect.

seeAlso.why: Error handling and retries
Error budgets that incidents consume

title: Autoscaling
objectives: Scale horizontally from a metric and target
Compute the replica count a proportional autoscaler chooses
Avoid flapping and slow cold starts

cards.title: Match capacity to demand
cards.body: An autoscaler adds instances when load rises and removes them when it falls, so you pay for what you use and keep latency steady. It works for stateless services that can run many identical copies behind a load balancer.

cards.title: Target tracking
cards.body: Most autoscalers keep a metric near a target: average CPU at 60%, or 100 requests a second per instance. If the metric is above target they add instances in proportion; below target they remove them, usually more cautiously.

cards.title: Worked example: the Kubernetes formula
cards.body: The horizontal pod autoscaler computes desired replicas = ceil(current replicas × current metric ÷ target).
steps: 4 replicas, average CPU 90%, target 60%
desired = ceil(4 × 90 ÷ 60) = ceil(6.0) = 6
Two new pods start; until they pass readiness, the old four carry the load
Later CPU falls to 30%: ceil(6 × 30 ÷ 60) = 3
Scale-down waits out a stabilisation window (5 minutes by default) so a brief dip does not remove pods too early

cards.title: Misconception: autoscaling handles any spike
cards.body: New instances take time: scheduling, pulling the image, starting the process, warming caches. A spike that doubles traffic in 30 seconds arrives before capacity does. Keep headroom, pre-scale for known events, and shed load when overwhelmed.

cards.title: Trap: scaling on the wrong metric
cards.body: A queue worker scaled on CPU may sit idle at low CPU while its queue grows, because it waits on a slow dependency. Scale on the signal that reflects backlog or demand, such as queue depth or requests per instance.

questions.prompt: A service runs 5 replicas at 84% average CPU with a 60% target. How many replicas does the proportional formula choose?
assumptions: desired = ceil(current × metric ÷ target)
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 7 replicas at the same total load average 5 × 84 ÷ 7 = 60% CPU, the target.

questions.prompt: Traffic triples in 20 seconds at a flash sale. Why might autoscaling not save the first minute?

choices.label: The autoscaler waits for the scale-down window first
New instances take time to start and warm
Scale-up is limited to one new instance per minute
Load balancers refuse to send traffic to new instances

questions.explanation: Even a fast decision needs minutes of boot, image pull and warm-up before new capacity serves. Scale-down windows only delay removing instances, scale-up rates are configurable rather than one a minute, and load balancers send traffic to new instances once their health checks pass.

questions.prompt: A queue worker waits on a slow API, so CPU stays at 15% while the backlog grows. What should it scale on?

choices.label: Queue depth per worker
Memory used per worker
Average CPU utilisation
Network bytes per second

questions.explanation: When work waits on I/O, CPU stays low while the backlog grows; queue depth per worker measures the waiting work directly. Memory and network bytes may not change with backlog, and CPU is the signal that is misleading here.

questions.prompt: Why do autoscalers scale down more slowly than up?

choices.label: To avoid flapping when load dips briefly
Scale-down needs a manual approval in most autoscalers
The metric is only collected every few minutes when load is low
Removing instances costs more money than adding them

questions.explanation: A stabilisation window avoids removing instances on a brief dip and adding them back moments later. Scale-down is automatic, metric collection does not slow at low load, and removing instances saves money rather than costing more.

questions.prompt: Order one autoscaling cycle.

items.label: New instances pass readiness and take traffic
Compare with the target and compute desired replicas
Create or remove instances
Collect the metric across replicas

questions.explanation: Measure, compute, act, become ready.

questions.prompt: A ticketing site expects a 10× spike when a concert goes on sale at 10:00.

approaches.label: Run 10× capacity all year
Scale out on a schedule before 10:00, with autoscaling and a queue as backup
Rely on CPU-based autoscaling alone

rationaleOptions.label: Reactive autoscaling is fast enough
Capacity is ready before the spike arrives
A waiting room absorbs any excess
Permanent peak capacity is the only safe choice

rationaleConflicts.r3: A 90 s cold start leaves the first minutes underprovisioned.
rationaleConflicts.r4: It costs about 10× for a few hours of need.

questions.explanation: For known events, pre-scale; keep reactive scaling for the unknown.

flashcards.back: desired = ceil(current replicas × current metric ÷ target).
To prevent flapping on brief dips.
Time from demand rising to new capacity serving traffic.

sources.title: Google Cloud: Autoscaling groups of instances

mechanism.title: What an autoscaler actually does
steps: Every period (15 seconds by default in Kubernetes) the autoscaler reads the metric for each replica, averages it, and computes the ratio to the target. If the ratio is within a tolerance (10% by default), it does nothing.

Otherwise it sets desired replicas proportionally, clamped between configured minimum and maximum counts. The maximum protects downstream systems and budgets; the minimum keeps enough capacity for sudden load and for losing a zone.
Scale-up is usually immediate; scale-down uses a stabilisation window that takes the highest recommendation over the last few minutes, so short dips do not remove capacity that will be needed again.

Cold start dominates response to spikes: node provisioning (if the cluster must grow too) can take minutes, image pulls seconds to minutes, and application warm-up more. Smaller images, warm pools of nodes and fast start-up all shorten it.

Metric choice matters: CPU suits CPU-bound services; request rate or concurrency per instance suits I/O-bound services; queue depth or age suits workers. Custom metrics need reliable pipelines, or the autoscaler acts on stale data.

Autoscaling interacts with everything downstream: doubling app instances doubles database connections and load on dependencies. Cap maximums to what dependencies can handle and protect them with pools and rate limits.

Cluster autoscalers add nodes when pods cannot be scheduled and remove under-used nodes, so pod autoscaling and node autoscaling work together; node scale-up is usually the slowest step and the main reason to keep spare capacity.

useWhen: Use autoscaling for stateless services with variable load.
Use scheduled scaling for known events.
Use queue-based scaling for background workers.
avoidWhen: Avoid scaling on metrics that do not reflect demand.
Avoid unbounded maximums that can overwhelm databases.
Avoid scaling stateful stores the same way as stateless services; they need data rebalancing.

numbers.title: Headroom against scaling lag
assumptions: Traffic can rise 40% within 2 minutes; new capacity needs 3 minutes to serve (illustrative)
Target CPU 60%
steps: During the 3-minute lag, existing instances must absorb the rise.
At 60% average, a 40% rise brings them to about 60% × 1.4 = 84%: still serving.
At an 80% target, the same rise would need 112%: overload and latency spikes.
Lower targets cost more instances but buy time for scaling to catch up.
numbers.result: The target utilisation is your headroom: set it from how fast load can rise versus how fast capacity arrives.

india.title: How the Kubernetes autoscaler decides
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Kubernetes documentation for horizontal pod autoscaling gives the algorithm as desiredReplicas = ceil[currentReplicas × (currentMetricValue ÷ desiredMetricValue)], skips scaling when the ratio is close enough to 1 (within a default tolerance of 0.1), and applies a default downscale stabilisation window of 300 seconds so that the number of replicas does not fluctuate frequently due to the dynamic nature of the metrics evaluated.

pitfalls.trap: “We have autoscaling, so spikes are handled.”
pitfalls.say: “Only spikes slower than our cold start; I’d keep headroom and pre-scale for known events.”

pitfalls.trap: “Scale everything on CPU.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d scale I/O-bound services on requests or queue depth, which reflect demand.”

takeaways: Autoscalers keep a metric near a target, proportionally.
Scale-down is deliberately slower to avoid flapping.
Cold-start time sets how much headroom you need.
Cap maximums to what dependencies can take.

interactive.title: What does the autoscaler pick?
interactive.prompt: An autoscaled API runs 8 replicas at 30% average CPU. The target is 60%, the minimum is 5 replicas, and the stabilisation window has passed.

choices.label: 4 by the formula, clamped up to the minimum of 5
choices.feedback: Right: ceil(8 × 30 ÷ 60) = 4, below the floor of 5.

choices.label: 4 replicas exactly
choices.feedback: The minimum replica setting overrides the formula.

choices.label: 8 replicas; it never scales down
choices.feedback: It scales down once the window has passed.

interactive.reveal: Minimum and maximum bounds clamp whatever the formula computes.
