Connection pools that scale with instance count

title: Cloud Networking: VPCs, Subnets and Security Groups
objectives: Lay out a VPC with public and private subnets
Tell stateful security groups from stateless network ACLs
Give private workloads outbound access without exposing them

cards.title: Your own private network in the cloud
cards.body: A virtual private cloud (VPC) is an isolated network with an address range you choose, such as 10.0.0.0/16. You divide it into subnets and attach route tables that decide where traffic goes. On AWS and Azure a subnet lives in one availability zone, so you create one per zone; on Google Cloud subnets are regional and span its zones.

cards.title: Public and private subnets
cards.body: A public subnet has a route to an internet gateway, so resources with public addresses can be reached from the internet. A private subnet does not; databases and application servers live there, reachable only from inside the VPC or through load balancers.

cards.title: Worked example: a three-tier layout
cards.body: A web application in two availability zones.
steps: VPC 10.0.0.0/16 split into public and private subnets in each zone
Public subnets: the load balancer and a NAT gateway
Private app subnets: servers whose security group accepts traffic only from the load balancer’s group
Private data subnets: the database, whose group accepts only the app servers’ group on the database port
App servers reach the internet for updates through the NAT gateway, which allows outbound connections only

cards.title: Misconception: private subnets cannot reach the internet
cards.body: They can initiate outbound connections through a NAT gateway; the internet just cannot start connections to them. That is usually what you want for updates and third-party APIs, but egress should still be restricted where data exfiltration matters.

cards.title: Trap: opening 0.0.0.0/0 on admin ports
cards.body: A security group that allows SSH or database ports from anywhere exposes them to constant internet scanning. Allow access from specific groups or ranges, and use a bastion or session manager for administration.

questions.prompt: What makes a subnet “public”?

choices.label: A route to an internet gateway
Its network ACL allows all inbound traffic
It hosts the NAT gateway
Its instances get public DNS names

questions.explanation: A subnet is public when its route table sends internet traffic to an internet gateway. An open network ACL still leaves no route out, a NAT gateway sits in a public subnet because it needs that route, and DNS names do not create reachability.

questions.prompt: A security group allows inbound port 443. Do responses need an outbound rule?

choices.label: Yes, unless the network ACL already allows it
Yes, each reply needs a rule
No, security groups are stateful
Only for responses to IPv6 clients

questions.explanation: Security groups are stateful: return traffic for an allowed connection is permitted without an outbound rule. Network ACLs are stateless and do need return rules, but that is a separate layer, and the behaviour is the same for IPv4 and IPv6.

questions.prompt: Private app servers must call a payment API on the internet. What gives them access without exposing them?

choices.label: Opening the security group to all
Public IPs on each server
Moving them to the public subnet
A NAT gateway in a public subnet

questions.explanation: A NAT gateway in a public subnet lets private servers start outbound connections while staying unreachable from outside. Public IPs, a move to the public subnet or an open security group all expose the servers to inbound traffic.

questions.prompt: How should the database’s security group allow the app servers?

choices.label: Allow 0.0.0.0/0 on the port
Allow the whole VPC range
Reference the app servers’ security group
Allow the NAT gateway’s public address on the port

questions.explanation: Referencing the app servers’ security group allows exactly those instances, even as they scale. 0.0.0.0/0 and the whole VPC range admit far more than the app tier, and the NAT gateway’s address is for outbound internet traffic, not internal calls.

questions.prompt: Order the path of a user request in a three-tier VPC.

items.label: App server to the database in a data subnet
Load balancer to an app server in a private subnet
Response returns along the same connection
Internet to the load balancer in a public subnet

questions.explanation: Edge, app, data, back.

questions.prompt: Engineers need occasional shell access to private servers.

approaches.label: A managed session service or bastion with logged, identity-based access
Share one SSH key on a wiki page
Open SSH to the internet with keys

rationaleOptions.label: Key-based SSH from anywhere is secure enough
No inbound ports open to the internet
A shared key is simpler to manage
Each session is tied to a person and logged

rationaleConflicts.r3: Exposed ports invite scanning and key theft is common.
rationaleConflicts.r4: It cannot be attributed or revoked per person.

questions.explanation: Broker admin access through identity and logging, not open ports.

flashcards.back: An isolated virtual network with your chosen address range.
Groups are stateful, allow-only, per resource; ACLs are stateless, allow and deny, per subnet.
Lets private resources start outbound connections without being reachable.

sources.title: AWS: Compare security groups and network ACLs

mechanism.title: How packets move inside a VPC
steps: Each subnet’s route table decides the next hop: local traffic within the VPC range stays inside; 0.0.0.0/0 goes to an internet gateway (public subnets) or a NAT gateway (private subnets); other routes may lead to peered VPCs or VPN connections.

Security groups attach to network interfaces and act as stateful firewalls: rules only allow, and if a connection is allowed in one direction, its replies are allowed back. Rules can reference other groups, so “app servers may reach the database” holds as instances come and go.

Network ACLs attach to subnets and are stateless: they evaluate inbound and outbound packets separately, support deny rules and are processed in rule-number order. They suit coarse subnet-wide blocks; most fine-grained control lives in security groups.

A NAT gateway translates private source addresses to its own public address for outbound connections and drops unsolicited inbound ones. It lives in a public subnet and is usually deployed per availability zone so one zone’s failure does not cut the others’ egress.
Private endpoints let workloads reach cloud services such as object storage without traversing the internet or a NAT gateway, which reduces cost and lets you restrict access to specific resources.
Plan address ranges up front: VPC and subnet ranges are hard to change, and overlapping ranges block peering and VPNs later. Leave space for more subnets and zones.

useWhen: Use private subnets for application and data tiers.
Use security-group references instead of IP ranges inside a VPC.
Use private endpoints for cloud services such as object storage to keep traffic off the internet.
avoidWhen: Avoid admin ports open to 0.0.0.0/0.
Avoid overlapping address ranges between networks you may connect.

numbers.title: Sizing subnets
assumptions: VPC 10.0.0.0/16; 3 zones × 3 tiers = 9 subnets of /20 (illustrative)
AWS reserves 5 addresses per subnet
steps: A /16 holds 65,536 addresses; a /20 holds 4,096.
Nine /20 subnets use 9 × 4,096 = 36,864 addresses, leaving room for more.
Each /20 gives 4,096 − 5 = 4,091 usable addresses on AWS.
Container platforms that give each pod a VPC address can use thousands of addresses per subnet, so size for pods, not servers.
numbers.result: Plan ranges for growth and for platforms that consume an address per pod.

india.title: Security groups and network ACLs in AWS
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: AWS’s VPC documentation compares the two controls: security groups operate at the instance level, support allow rules only and are stateful, so return traffic is automatically allowed; network ACLs operate at the subnet level, support allow and deny rules, are stateless so return traffic must be explicitly allowed, and process rules in order starting with the lowest number. AWS recommends using security groups as the primary control and ACLs as an additional layer.

pitfalls.trap: “It’s in a private subnet, so it’s safe.”
pitfalls.say: “Private stops inbound internet access; I’d still restrict security groups and egress.”

pitfalls.trap: “Allow the whole VPC range to the database.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d reference the app tier’s security group so only the app servers can connect.”

takeaways: VPCs split into public and private subnets per zone.
Security groups: stateful, allow-only, per interface.
NAT gives private workloads outbound-only access.
Plan address ranges for growth and peering.

interactive.title: Can the database be reached from the internet?
interactive.prompt: The database sits in a private subnet with no internet gateway route. Its security group allows port 5432 from 0.0.0.0/0.

choices.label: Not directly: there is no route from the internet, but the rule is still too broad
choices.feedback: Right: routing blocks the internet, but any VPC resource can connect.

choices.label: Yes: the security group allows everyone
choices.feedback: Without a route, internet packets never arrive.

choices.label: No, and the rule is harmless
choices.feedback: A compromised resource inside the VPC can reach it.

interactive.reveal: Use routing and narrow security groups together; neither alone is enough.

Egress rules and private subnets that limit SSRF

title: Backups and Disaster Recovery
objectives: Define RPO and RTO and pick strategies that meet them
Design backups that survive deletion, ransomware and regional loss
Test restores and failovers regularly

cards.title: Two numbers drive the design
cards.body: The recovery point objective (RPO) is how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. The recovery time objective (RTO) is how long you can be down. A nightly backup gives an RPO of up to 24 hours; continuous replication gives seconds.

cards.title: Replicas are not backups
cards.body: Replication copies every change, including mistakes: a dropped table or encrypted files arrive at the replica within seconds. Backups are point-in-time copies kept separately, so you can go back to before the mistake.

cards.title: Worked example: a point-in-time restore
cards.body: A bad migration deletes a column at 14:05.
steps: Identify the last good moment: 14:04
Restore the most recent full backup (from 02:00) to a new instance
Replay write-ahead logs from 02:00 to 14:04
Verify the data, then copy the missing column back or switch the app over
Record the restore time; it is a real measurement of your RTO

cards.title: Misconception: backups exist, so we can recover
cards.body: A backup that has never been restored is a hope. Backups fail silently: wrong paths, expired credentials, missing encryption keys. Only regular restore tests prove both that data is there and how long recovery takes.

cards.title: Trap: backups reachable with production credentials
cards.body: If the same credentials that run production can delete backups, ransomware or an attacker deletes both. Keep copies in a separate account with immutable (write-once) retention, and at least one copy in another region.

questions.prompt: A business can lose at most 15 minutes of orders. Which objective is that?

choices.label: Mean time between failures
Recovery time objective
Recovery point objective
Service level indicator

questions.explanation: The recovery point objective is the most data, measured in time, you can afford to lose. The recovery time objective is how long recovery may take, mean time between failures measures failure frequency, and an SLI measures service quality.

questions.prompt: Someone runs DROP TABLE on the primary. What happens on a synchronous replica?

choices.label: The replica keeps the table
The replica rejects the change
The table is dropped there too
The replica pauses replication

questions.explanation: Replicas copy every committed change, so the drop reaches the synchronous replica too; only a backup or point-in-time restore lets you go back. Replicas do not keep, reject or pause on valid statements.

questions.prompt: What best protects backups from ransomware that holds admin credentials?

choices.label: Compressing the backup files
Daily backups kept in the same account as production
Encrypting the backups with a key in the production account
Immutable copies in a separate account

questions.explanation: Immutable copies in a separate account cannot be deleted with the production admin credentials an attacker holds. Compression changes nothing, and backups or keys in the same account are within the attacker’s reach.

questions.prompt: Which strategy gives the lowest RTO?

choices.label: Pilot light
Backup and restore
Warm standby scaled down in a second region
Active-active in two regions

questions.explanation: Active-active already serves traffic in both regions, so recovery is mostly shifting load. Warm standby must scale up, pilot light must start most services, and backup and restore must rebuild everything, each with a longer RTO.

questions.prompt: Order DR strategies from slowest to fastest recovery.

items.label: Multi-site active-active
Pilot light
Warm standby
Backup and restore

questions.explanation: More pre-provisioned capacity means faster recovery at higher cost.

questions.prompt: An internal reporting tool can be down for a day and lose a day of data; a payments service needs RTO under 15 minutes and RPO near zero.

approaches.label: Active-active for both services
Nightly backups for both services
Backup and restore for reporting; warm standby with replication for payments

rationaleOptions.label: Payments meets its tight RTO and RPO
Uniform DR is simpler, so use the strongest everywhere
Spend matches each service’s objectives
Nightly backups are fine if restores are practised

rationaleConflicts.r3: It multiplies cost for services that do not need it.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Restore takes hours and loses up to a day: too much for payments.

questions.explanation: Set RPO and RTO per service and pick the cheapest strategy that meets them.

flashcards.back: Maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time.
Maximum acceptable downtime.
Replicas copy mistakes immediately; backups keep earlier points in time.

sources.title: AWS: Disaster recovery options in the cloud
PostgreSQL: Continuous Archiving and Point-in-Time Recovery
Google Cloud: Disaster recovery planning guide

mechanism.title: Building recovery you can trust
steps: Start from the business: for each service, agree RPO and RTO with its owners. These numbers decide the strategy and the cost; without them, teams either overspend or discover the gap during a disaster.

Backups: take full or incremental snapshots on a schedule, plus continuous log archiving for databases to allow point-in-time recovery. Encrypt them, keep the keys recoverable separately, and copy them to another region and another account.

Immutability: object-lock or write-once retention prevents deletion or modification until the retention period ends, even by administrators. This defeats ransomware and insider mistakes that target backups.

Strategies, from cheapest to fastest: backup and restore (hours), pilot light (core data replicated, servers off until needed), warm standby (a scaled-down copy running), and multi-site active-active (full capacity in each region, failover in seconds to minutes).

Dependencies matter: a recovered service also needs DNS, identity, secrets, configuration and its upstream and downstream services in the recovery region. Infrastructure as code and documented runbooks make the recovery environment reproducible.

Test: restore backups to a scratch environment on a schedule and verify the data; run failover game days. Measure actual RPO and RTO and compare with the objectives; untested plans usually take far longer than written.

Retention follows both recovery needs and rules: keep frequent recent copies for quick restores and fewer older copies for audits or late-discovered corruption, and delete data that law or policy says must not be kept longer.

useWhen: Use point-in-time recovery for databases holding business data.
Use immutable, cross-account, cross-region backup copies.
Use scheduled restore tests whose results are reported like any other metric.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating replicas or RAID as backups.
Avoid DR plans that have never been exercised.

numbers.title: How long a restore really takes
assumptions: Database size 2 TB; restore throughput 200 MB/s; 6 hours of logs to replay at 10× real time (illustrative)
steps: Copying 2 TB at 200 MB/s: 2,000,000 MB ÷ 200 = 10,000 s, about 2.8 hours.
Replaying 6 hours of logs at 10× takes about 36 minutes.
Add verification and switching the application over: say 30 minutes.
Total about 3.9 hours: if the RTO is 1 hour, backup and restore cannot meet it.
numbers.result: Compute RTO from data size and throughput; large databases often need replicas or standby to meet tight targets.

india.title: A data centre fire
india.label: Publicly reported
india.body: Publicly reported by OVHcloud in March 2021: a fire destroyed one data centre building at its Strasbourg site and damaged another, and the site was shut down. Customers whose only backups were stored in the same site lost data permanently, while those with copies in other regions could rebuild. The event is widely cited as a reminder that backups must be stored away from the systems they protect.

pitfalls.trap: “We have a replica, so we have backups.”
pitfalls.say: “A replica copies a dropped table in seconds; I’d keep point-in-time backups separately too.”

pitfalls.trap: “Our RTO is one hour.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d check that against a timed restore; a 2 TB database can take hours to copy back.”

takeaways: Set RPO and RTO per service, then choose the strategy.
Replicas are not backups; keep point-in-time copies.
Make backups immutable and store them in another account and region.
Test restores and failovers; measure real times.

interactive.title: Can they recover?
interactive.prompt: Ransomware with domain admin rights encrypts production servers and deletes the backup vault in the same cloud account. A weekly copy also goes to object storage with 30-day object lock in another account.

choices.label: Yes, from the locked copy, losing up to a week of data
choices.feedback: Right: the immutable copy survives, but its RPO is a week.

choices.label: No: the attacker deleted all backups
choices.feedback: The locked copy in another account cannot be deleted.

choices.label: Yes, with no data loss
choices.feedback: The latest locked copy can be up to 7 days old.

interactive.reveal: Immutable, separate copies make recovery possible; their schedule sets how much you lose.

seeAlso.why: Replication is not a backup
Write-ahead logs make point-in-time recovery possible
